1.1.l: Pediatric Hip — Approach to the Pediatric Hip & the Limping Child
1.1.b:
Every child's hip case starts with the same three questions, whatever the disease turns out to be.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you approach a limping child?"
- "**Age** first: what is common is common for that age."
- "Read **pain and gait together**: pain is the commonest cause of a limp."
- "Exclude the **red flags**, above all septic arthritis, in every case."

### The Limping Child
The term is wider than the hip.
- "Limping child" covers pain anywhere from hip to foot (Handbook)
- The hip is the commonest source, so it is examined first
- Three presentations: **pain**, **limp**, and **leg-length difference**
- Begin with pain, then the limp, then the cause of the limp

### Three Age Groups
Any disease can appear at any age, but each age has its own usual suspects.

| Age group | Most likely | Must not miss |
|---|---|---|
| **0–2 years** | DDH (developmental dysplasia of the hip), transient synovitis | septic arthritis, non-accidental injury |
| **3–9 years** | Perthes disease, transient synovitis | septic arthritis, leukaemia |
| **10–16 years** | SCFE (slipped capital femoral epiphysis), AVN (avascular necrosis), trauma | septic arthritis, malignancy |

- The groups follow the lecture slide (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Perthes after **12 years** behaves as juvenile AVN, not Perthes

### Knee Pain Is Hip Pain
A child's hip often hurts in the knee.
- The **obturator nerve** supplies both the hip and the knee
[[FIG: Fig 1.1 · 1.1
- SCFE is missed when the child presents with knee pain (Miller)

PITFALL — the child with knee pain
- The knee is normal on examination and on every scan
- Say → "**I examine the hip first and X-ray the pelvis, not only the knee**"

MEMORY HOOK — the knee tells tales
- The knee is the hip's loud neighbour: it complains, but the trouble lives next door.

1.2.l: Pediatric Hip — Approach to the Pediatric Hip & the Limping Child
1.2.b:
The child's hip changes with age, and each age has its own weak point.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "blood supply of the child's femoral head"
- "Infant: **metaphyseal vessels** still cross the physis."
- "From 4 years: the MFCA (medial femoral circumflex artery) **lateral epiphyseal vessels** alone."
- "After physeal closure: metaphyseal anastomoses return."

### Ossification of the Proximal Femur
The head starts as cartilage and ossifies from one centre.
- Femoral head nucleus appears at **4–7 months**, earlier in girls
[[FIG: Fig 1.2 · 1.2
- Greater trochanter apophysis ossifies at ≈**4 years**
- Lesser trochanter ossifies near **10 years**
- A late or small nucleus on one side is abnormal → 02 DDH Pathology

#### Growth Plates
- The **proximal femoral physis** grows the neck in length
- It gives ≈**30%** of femoral length and ≈3 mm a year
- The **trochanteric apophysis** grows the greater trochanter
- Head physis arrest with a growing trochanter: **coxa vara**, high trochanter

### The Acetabulum
The socket grows from a Y-shaped cartilage.
- **Triradiate cartilage** joins ilium, ischium and pubis in the floor
- It closes at bone age **11–13** in girls and **13–15** in boys (Campbell)
- Head and socket shape each other: a seated head builds a deep socket
- Growth centres and their damage → 02 DDH Pathology

### Blood Supply of the Femoral Head by Age
Trueta showed that the supply changes as the physis matures.

| Age | Main supply |
|---|---|
| **Infant** | metaphyseal vessels cross the physis; MFCA, LFCA (lateral femoral circumflex artery), ligamentum teres |
| **≈4 years** | LFCA and ligamentum teres regress; physis blocks metaphyseal vessels |
| **4 years to physeal closure** | MFCA retinacular branches, the **lateral epiphyseal vessels**, almost alone |
| **After physeal closure** | metaphyseal–epiphyseal anastomoses develop |

- Table after Miller's age table and Trueta (Miller)
- The **posterosuperior retinacular** branches run up the back of the neck
[[FIG: Fig 1.3 · 1.2
- They are intracapsular, so pressure or a slip can kink them

#### Why It Matters at Each Age
- **Infant**: shared vessels let metaphyseal pus enter the epiphysis and joint
[[FIG: Fig 1.4 · 1.2
- **4–8 years**: the supply is deficient, the Perthes window (Trueta)
[[FIG: Fig 1.5 · 1.2
- **Adolescent**: an unstable SCFE tears the retinacular vessels → AVN (avascular necrosis)
- **Any age**: a tense effusion squeezes the retinacular vessels → urgent drainage

#### Intracapsular Metaphysis
- The hip capsule attaches below the physis, on the neck
[[FIG: Fig 1.6 · 1.2
- Metaphyseal osteomyelitis therefore bursts straight into the joint
- Same pattern: shoulder, elbow (radial neck) and ankle (lateral malleolus)

PITFALL — "why does osteomyelitis cause septic arthritis?"
- Two reasons are asked: the intracapsular metaphysis and the infant's transphyseal vessels
- Say → "**Infants, and joints with an intracapsular metaphysis: hip, shoulder, elbow, ankle**"

MEMORY HOOK — the lonely artery
- From 4 to 8 the head hangs on one lifeline; cut it and Perthes moves in.

1.3.l: Pediatric Hip — Approach to the Pediatric Hip & the Limping Child
1.3.b:
A complete history tells the examiner you know why each question is asked.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what do you ask?"
- "Age, sex, pain site and timing, fever, trauma."
- "Birth and family history, activity and weight."
- "Drugs and hormones: steroids, growth hormone, endocrine disease."

### Age and Sex
The first two facts already narrow the list.
- **DDH**: girls, about five to one
- **Perthes**: boys, peak **4–8 years**
- **SCFE**: boys, obese, around the growth spurt
- **Transient synovitis**: boys, peak 4–8 years, like Perthes

### Pain
Ask where, when and how it behaves.
- **Site**: groin, thigh or knee; ask how far it spreads
- **Activity pain**: mechanical, worse with use
- **Morning pain and limp** that improve with walking: inflammatory
- Inflammatory: transient synovitis, juvenile arthritis, Perthes synovitis (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- **Night pain** or weight loss: tumour or leukaemia until proven otherwise

### Fever, Infection and Trauma
These questions catch the emergencies.
- Recent upper respiratory or urinary infection: blood-borne infection
- Fever with refusal to bear weight: septic arthritis
- Recent antibiotics may **mask** septic arthritis (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Trauma: fracture, or **non-accidental injury** in the toddler

### Birth and Family History
Some diseases run in families; some start at delivery.
- **Breech** delivery and first-born: DDH
- NICU (neonatal intensive care unit) stay with lines: neonatal septic hip
- Family history: **DDH** strongly, SCFE occasionally (Miller)
- Perthes: a weak family link only, unlike DDH

### Activity, Weight and Drugs
Body build and medicines point to particular diseases.
- A very active, small boy: Perthes
- An obese, less active adolescent: SCFE
- **Steroids** (asthma, nephrotic syndrome): AVN of the head
- **Growth hormone**, hypothyroidism, renal failure: SCFE (Miller)

| Question | Why it is asked |
|---|---|
| Age | category: what is common is common |
| Sex | DDH in girls; Perthes and SCFE in boys |
| Pain timing | morning → inflammatory; night → tumour |
| Fever, infection | septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, transient synovitis |
| Birth, breech | DDH |
| Family | DDH, SCFE |
| Activity, weight | Perthes active; SCFE obese |
| Steroids, hormones | AVN; SCFE |

PITFALL — the missing question
- Each skipped item invites "why did you not ask?" (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Say → "**I cover the whole checklist, and I know why each item is there**"

1.4.l: Pediatric Hip — Approach to the Pediatric Hip & the Limping Child
1.4.b:
The examination follows look, gait, feel, move and measure, then the joints above and below.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "the four limps"
- "**Antalgic**: short stance on the painful limb."
- "**Trendelenburg**: the sound side drops; the trunk leans to the weak side."
- "**Short-limb** dip, and **waddling** when both hips are weak."

### Attitude of the Irritable Hip
The resting position tells you the joint is tense.
- Hip held in **flexion, abduction and external rotation**
[[FIG: Fig 1.7 · 1.4
- In this position the capsule holds the most fluid
- Seen in septic arthritis and transient synovitis
- **Pseudoparalysis**: the infant will not move the septic limb

### Gait
Name the gait in exam words, not with your hands.
- Stance phase occupies **60%** of the gait cycle (Miller)
[[FIG: Fig 1.8 · 1.4
- Swing is the remaining **40%**

#### Antalgic Gait
- Definition: **short stance phase** on the painful limb (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 1.9 · 1.4
- The step on the sound side is quick, to unload the sore side
- From a hip, the trunk shifts over the hip without pelvic drop: **coxalgic gait**

#### Trendelenburg Gait
- Cause: **abductor weakness** (gluteus medius and minimus)
- In stance on the weak side the **sound side sinks** in swing
[[FIG: Fig 1.10 · 1.4
- The trunk lurches **towards the affected side** to balance
- This lurch is the **abductor lurch**

#### Short-Limb Gait
- The pelvis **dips** on the short side at each step
- Compensation: equinus of the short limb or a bent long knee
[[FIG: Fig 1.11 · 1.4
- A dip means a short limb; a lurch means an unstable hip

#### Waddling Gait
- **Bilateral Trendelenburg**: the trunk swings to each side
[[FIG: Fig 1.12 · 1.4
- Classic in bilateral DDH, also in coxa vara and myopathies

#### Rotational Gaits
- **Out-toeing** with a limp in an adolescent: SCFE
- **In-toeing** in a child under 10: femoral anteversion

| Gait | Cause | What you see |
|---|---|---|
| **Antalgic** | pain | short stance on the sore limb |
| **Trendelenburg** | abductor weakness | sound side sinks; trunk lurches to the weak side |
| **Short-limb** | leg-length difference | pelvic dip, equinus |
| **Waddling** | bilateral abductor weakness | trunk swings both ways |

MEMORY HOOK — dip or lurch
- A short leg dips like a boat in a wave; a weak hip lurches like a drunk sailor.

### Trendelenburg Test
The test shows whether the abductors hold the pelvis level.
- The child stands on one leg, the other hip and knee flexed
[[FIG: Fig 1.13 · 1.4
- Normal: the pelvis on the lifted side **rises**
- Positive: it **drops**, more than 2 cm (Campbell)

#### Causes of a Positive Test
- **Weak abductors**: polio, myopathy, L5 root or superior gluteal nerve palsy
[[FIG: Fig 1.14 · 1.4
- **Short lever arm**: coxa vara, high trochanter
- **Lost fulcrum**: dislocated hip, as in DDH
- **Pain** in the hip inhibits the abductors

### Range of Movement
Compare both sides; loss of internal rotation is the earliest sign.
- **Internal rotation** goes first in nearly every hip disease
- Perthes: limited **abduction** and internal rotation (Handbook)
- SCFE: **obligatory external rotation** on flexion, the Drehmann sign → 09 SCFE
- Hinge abduction in Perthes → 06 Perthes Treatment

#### Log Roll
- Roll the straight leg gently inwards and outwards
[[FIG: Fig 1.15 · 1.4
- It moves only the femoral head in the socket
- Guarding on rolling is a specific sign of an irritable hip

#### Thomas Test
- Flex the opposite hip fully to flatten the lumbar lordosis
[[FIG: Fig 1.16 · 1.4
- The tested thigh rises off the couch: **fixed flexion deformity**
- Seen with effusion, septic arthritis and psoas irritation (Handbook)

### Rotational Profile
Staheli's profile measures femoral and tibial twist separately.

| Measurement | Normal | Abnormal means |
|---|---|---|
| **Foot-progression angle** | −5° to +20° | nonspecific |
| **Internal rotation, prone** | 20–60° | >70°: femoral anteversion |
| **External rotation, prone** | 30–60° | <20°: femoral anteversion |
| **Thigh–foot angle** | 0–20° | <−10°: internal tibial torsion |

- Values from Miller's Table 3.2
[[FIG: Fig 1.17 · 1.4
- Anteverted femur → toe-in; retroverted femur → toe-out
[[FIG: Fig 1.18 · 1.4

#### Femoral Anteversion
- At birth anteversion is ≈**30–40°**; it falls to ≈15° at maturity
- The child sits in a **W position** and walks with patellae turned in
[[FIG: Fig 1.19 · 1.4
- Most resolve spontaneously by **10 years**

#### Tibial Torsion
- Prone, knees bent: the **thigh–foot angle**
[[FIG: Fig 1.20 · 1.4
- Internal tibial torsion is the common toddler cause of in-toeing

### Leg Length
Measure true and apparent length, then find the level of shortening.
- **True length**: ASIS (anterior superior iliac spine) to medial malleolus
[[FIG: Fig 1.21 · 1.4
- **Apparent length**: xiphisternum or umbilicus to medial malleolus
- Square the pelvis and match the good leg's position first
- Apparent shortening with equal true lengths: **adduction deformity** or pelvic tilt
[[FIG: Fig 1.22 · 1.4

#### Galeazzi Test
- Supine, hips and knees flexed, feet together on the couch
[[FIG: Fig 1.23 · 1.4
- The lower knee is on the **short** side
- Positive in any femoral shortening: DDH, short femur, coxa vara, physeal arrest
- Bilateral dislocation may look level: a **false negative**

#### Neonatal Tests
- **Barlow** tests dislocatability of a located hip
[[FIG: Fig 1.24 · 1.4
- **Ortolani** tests reducibility of a dislocated hip
- Technique and meaning → 02 DDH Pathology

#### Beyond the Hip
- Examine the **spine**: discitis or a neural cause of limp
- Examine the knee, leg and foot: toddler fracture, osteomyelitis
- Abdomen and nodes: a psoas abscess, appendicitis, or leukaemia

PITFALL — the term you cannot define
- Saying "hinge abduction" leads the examiner straight to it (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Say → "**I only name a sign I can define and demonstrate**"

MEMORY HOOK — the shy internal rotator
- Internal rotation is the hip's shyest movement: at the first sign of trouble, it hides.

- "**AP (anteroposterior) pelvis and frog lateral** of both hips."
- "**Ultrasound** for an effusion and to guide aspiration."
- "**MRI** for early AVN, osteomyelitis, or a pre-slip."

### Plain Radiographs
Both hips on one film let you compare.
- **AP pelvis**: legs internally rotated 15–20°
- **Frog lateral**: hips abducted and flexed
[[FIG: Fig 1.25 · 1.5
- A visible **lesser trochanter** means the leg was externally rotated
[[FIG: Fig 1.26 · 1.5
- External rotation gives a false look of **coxa valga** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)

#### Reading a Child's Pelvis Film
- Name the view, side and open physes: "skeletally immature pelvis"
- Ossific nucleus: present, size, density, fragmentation
- Head position: lines and quadrants
- Physis: width, irregularity, the epiphyseal height
- Metaphysis: widening, cysts, blanch
- Acetabulum: index, shape, congruence with the head

|---|---|---|

| **Shenton** | continuity neck–obturator arc | 02 DDH Pathology |
| **Acetabular index**, CE (centre-edge) angle | socket depth, coverage | 02 DDH Pathology |
| **Lateral pillar** | Perthes severity | 05 Perthes Pathology |
| **Klein line** | slip on the AP | 09 SCFE |
| **Southwick angle** | slip on the frog lateral | 09 SCFE |
| **Hilgenreiner–epiphyseal angle** | coxa vara | 10 Coxa Vara |

- DDH film: small nucleus, superolateral head, broken Shenton line
[[FIG: Fig 1.27 · 1.5

- **Klein line**: along the superior neck; it should cut the epiphysis

### Ultrasound
Ultrasound is the quickest test for an effusion.
- It detects intracapsular fluid with high sensitivity
[[FIG: Fig 1.30 · 1.5
- It cannot tell pus from serous fluid (Handbook)
- It guides **aspiration**, the definitive test
- Normal: the capsule hugs the neck with no fluid gap

### MRI and Other Tests
MRI shows what the film misses.
- Effusion, synovitis and early **osteomyelitis** or abscess
[[FIG: Fig 1.31 · 1.5
- Early AVN before the film changes: Perthes and juvenile AVN
- The contralateral **pre-slip** in SCFE
- Bone scan: localises an obscure limp, or a cold head in early Perthes
[[FIG: Fig 1.32 · 1.5
- CT: bony detail, for example an osteoid osteoma nidus

#### Laboratory Tests
- WBC (white blood cell count), ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), CRP (C-reactive protein)
- Raised in septic arthritis and osteomyelitis, normal in Perthes and SCFE
- Full blood picture and film: leukaemia

### Causes of a Painful Hip
| Condition | Key clue | Home |
|---|---|---|
| **Transient synovitis** | commonest; afebrile or low fever; better in days | 07 Septic Hip |
| **Septic arthritis** | fever, refuses to bear weight, raised CRP | 07 Septic Hip |
| **Osteomyelitis** of proximal femur | fever, deep bone pain, patchy sclerosis later | 07 Septic Hip |
| **DDH** | painless limp, short leg, waddling | 02 DDH Pathology |
| **Perthes disease** | boy 4–8, insidious limp, fragmented head | 05 Perthes Pathology |
| **SCFE** | obese adolescent, knee pain, external rotation | 09 SCFE |
| **Coxa vara** | painless waddling, Trendelenburg | 10 Coxa Vara |
| **MED** (multiple epiphyseal dysplasia) | short stature, symmetrical bilateral heads | this chapter |
| **Leukaemia**, tumour | night pain, cytopenia, systemic illness | this chapter |

#### Transient Synovitis
- The **most common** cause of a painful hip under 10 years (Handbook)
- Must improve within **3 days**; resolves in 1–2 weeks (Handbook)
- A diagnosis of exclusion; ESR usually under 20 mm/hr (Miller)

#### Septic Arthritis
- The hip is the commonest site in children; *Staphylococcus aureus* commonest (Handbook)
- Infant film: lateral displacement of the femur from a tense effusion
[[FIG: Fig 1.33 · 1.6
- Kocher criteria and drainage → 07 Septic Hip

#### Multiple Epiphyseal Dysplasia
- Bilateral, **symmetrical** irregular heads that mimic Perthes
[[FIG: Fig 1.34 · 1.6
- Short stature, other epiphyses involved, "double-layer" patella

#### Leukaemia and Tumours
- Acute leukaemia can present as bone pain and limp
[[FIG: Fig 1.35 · 1.6
- Clues: night pain, pallor, bruising, fever, abnormal blood film
- Femoral neck osteoid osteoma: night pain eased by NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs)
- It may present as a painless limp with synovitis
[[FIG: Fig 1.36 · 1.6

#### Signs Not to Confuse
- The Handbook lists the blanch sign and V-sign under Perthes
- **Gage sign**: a V-shaped lucency at the lateral epiphysis in Perthes
[[FIG: Fig 1.37 · 1.6
- It is a Catterall head-at-risk sign (Miller)
- The **blanch sign** of Steel belongs to SCFE → 09 SCFE

#### Other Causes
- Osteomyelitis elsewhere in the limb, for example the tibia
[[FIG: Fig 1.38 · 1.6
- Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: morning stiffness, effusion with synovitis
[[FIG: Fig 1.39 · 1.6
- Discitis, psoas abscess, appendicitis: referred hip pain
- Toddler's fracture of the tibia: the toddler who will not walk
[[FIG: Fig 1.40 · 1.6

1.7.l: Pediatric Hip — Approach to the Pediatric Hip & the Limping Child
1.7.b:
The exam wants a diagnostic scheme, not a list of essays.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how to answer 'differential diagnosis of the limping child'"
- "List the causes with one line each."
- "Then give a **scheme**: history → examination → labs → imaging."
- "At each step say which result points to which cause."

### Answering the Question
The Handbook's three steps turn a list into an answer.
- **List** the causes briefly (Handbook)
- **Outline** the diagnostic scheme
- **Correlate** each expected result with its cause

#### Two More Handbook Rules
- "Management" means diagnosis **and** treatment, not treatment alone (Handbook)
- Put each classification where it belongs: imaging classes under imaging
- Example: name the Aitken type when imaging PFFD (proximal femoral focal deficiency) → 10 Coxa Vara

### The Diagnostic Scheme
Each step filters the list.

| Step | Finding | Suspect |
|---|---|---|
| **History** | prior infection | septic arthritis, osteomyelitis |
| | trauma | fracture, non-accidental injury |
| **Examination** | pain, swelling, tenderness | septic arthritis, osteomyelitis |
| | limited abduction and internal rotation | Perthes |
| | Thomas sign | effusion, septic arthritis |
| **Labs** | raised WBC, ESR, CRP | infection |
| **X-ray** | rounding of the epiphysis | transient synovitis |
| | patchy sclerosis | osteomyelitis |
| | fragmentation, metaphyseal cyst | Perthes |
| | displacement signs | SCFE |

### Septic Arthritis or Transient Synovitis
This is the decision that cannot wait.

| Kocher predictor | Positive when |
|---|---|
| **Fever** | >38.5°C |
| **Non-weight-bearing** | the child cannot bear weight |
| **ESR** | >40 mm/hr |
| **WBC** | >12,000 cells/mm³ |

- Four predictors: probability of sepsis ≈**99%** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Three predictors: ≈**93%**
- CRP above **20 mg/L** adds strongly to the picture
- Details, CRP rule and treatment → 07 Septic Hip

### Stepwise Plan for the Irritable Hip
The Handbook's flow for transient synovitis is the safe default.
- Hip pain, no red flags: observe closely for **1–2 days** (Handbook)
- Pain beyond **2 days**: X-ray to exclude other disease
- Suspected effusion: ultrasound
- Fever, high markers or a tense effusion: **aspirate**; pus means septic arthritis

### Presenting a Hip Case
The examiner follows the order you choose.
- History → examination → **septic arthritis excluded** → X-ray → plan → complications
- No hip case passes without excluding sepsis (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Read the film logically: an abnormal Klein line is SCFE, not "AVN"

PITFALL — the antibiotic-masked hip
- Empirical antibiotics soften the picture of septic arthritis
- Say → "**On antibiotics, a calm-looking hip can still be septic: I aspirate**"

MEMORY HOOK — the three Ls
- List, Lay out, Link: three Ls turn a list of diseases into a pass.

| Age groups | 0–2 · 3–9 · 10–16 years |

| Proximal femoral physis | ≈30% of femoral length |

| Perthes window (Trueta) | 4–8 years |
| Stance phase | 60% of the gait cycle |
| Trendelenburg positive | pelvis drops >2 cm |
| Internal rotation prone | 20–60°; >70° anteversion |
| Thigh–foot angle | 0–20° |

| CRP septic | >20 mg/L |
